q: 201. The most suitable excreta disposal unit for human excreta is
explain: A privy pit (latrine pit) is a basic and common method for the direct disposal of human excreta in areas without a piped sewerage system.

q: 202. The underground structure in the form of a circular or rectangular tank for the purposes of admitting sewage into it from the intercepting chamber is called a
explain: A cesspool is a watertight underground tank used for the temporary collection and storage of sewage; it must be emptied periodically.

q: 203. The percentage ratio of the oxygen available in sewage to the oxygen required to satisfy one stage of bio-chemical oxygen demand (B.O.D.) is termed as
explain: Relative stability indicates the ability of an effluent to resist putrefaction, expressed as the ratio of available oxygen to the total oxygen required for BOD.

q: 204. In preliminary treatment of sewage, the operation which takes place, is
options: removal of fine dissolved organic material
removal of harmful bacteria and other organisms
explain: Preliminary treatment involves physical processes like screening and skimming to remove large floating objects and lighter materials like grease or oil.

q: 205. In secondary treatment of sewage, the operation which takes place is
options: removal of heavier suspended inorganic material
removal of fine dissolved organic material
explain: Secondary treatment is biological; it uses microorganisms to decompose and remove dissolved and colloidal organic matter from the sewage.

q: 206. The secondary treatment of sewage is carried out by the use of
explain: Trickling filters (and activated sludge processes) are biological units used in secondary treatment to oxidize organic matter.

q: 207. In primary settling tank, suspended solids are reduced from
explain: A well-designed primary sedimentation tank can remove approximately 40-70% of the suspended solids through gravity settling.

q: 208. In high rate activated sludge treatment, bacteria are removed from
explain: Activated sludge plants are highly efficient, typically achieving 80-95% removal of bacteria and BOD.

q: 209. Grit chambers of a sewage plant are usually changed after
explain: Depending on the accumulation rate, grit is typically cleaned or removed from the chambers every 2 weeks to maintain efficiency.

q: 210. Grit should be removed from sewage before
options: their lifting by means of pump etc.
settling of sewage in sedimentation tank
explain: Grit removal is essential to protect pumps from abrasion, prevent pipe clogging, and ensure that primary sedimentation tanks are not filled with inorganic matter.

q: 211. Biological action is used in
explain: Trickling filters rely on a biological slime layer (biofilm) of aerobic bacteria to consume organic contaminants.

q: 212. The sewage is treated by aerobic bacteria action in
explain: Aerobic processes occur in trickling filters, oxidation ponds (upper layers), and even to a degree in secondary settling tanks if oxygen is present.

q: 213. The privy pit should be located at least................ from the well or other ground water supply
explain: A distance of 30 meters is a standard safety guideline to prevent the seepage of pathogens from the pit into drinking water sources.

q: 214. A septic tank is a
options: combination of sedimentation and digestion tank
explain: A septic tank performs two functions: it allows solids to settle (sedimentation) and then allows anaerobic bacteria to break them down (digestion).

q: 215. The effluents from the septic tank are discharged into
explain: Because septic tank effluent is still partially polluted, it is typically discharged into a soak pit or dispersion trench for ground absorption.

q: 216. The equipment used for removing paper and rags from sewers is called
explain: A claw is a specialized tool used in sewer maintenance to snag and pull out rags, paper, or fibrous materials causing blockages.

q: 217. The equipment used for cleaning the sewers easily is called
explain: Scrapers are pushed or pulled through sewers to remove accumulated silt and deposits from the pipe walls.

q: 218. Land disposal of sewage will be favorable where
options: the rivers run dry or have a small flow during summer
climate is wet and rates of evaporation is low
explain: Land disposal (irrigation) is preferred when the receiving water bodies do not have enough volume (dilution capacity) to handle the sewage.

q: 219. Disposal by dilution will be suitable where
options: the sewage arriving at the out fall points is fresh
explain: Dilution works best when water is moving away, not returning to the shore, and when the sewage is fresh (hasn't become septic/odorous).

q: 220. When the sewage is to be distributed over a level area surrounded by dykes, the method is called
explain: Flooding involves applying sewage to a leveled area enclosed by small embankments (dykes) to allow it to seep into the soil.

q: 221. The natural process in which the oxygen of water of streams is consumed and replenished by the atmosphere is
explain: Self-purification is the natural ability of a river to recover its dissolved oxygen and water quality through physical and biological processes.

q: 222. The minimum dissolved oxygen required in water to save the aquatic life is
explain: Fish and other aquatic organisms generally require a minimum of 4 ppm (or mg/L) of dissolved oxygen to survive.

q: 223. The bio-chemical treatment of sewage effluent is a process of
explain: Biological treatment uses bacteria to oxidize organic matter into stable inorganic compounds.

q: 224. The amount of oxygen consumed by sewage from an oxidizing agent like potassium dichromate is
explain: COD measures the oxygen equivalent of the organic matter in a sample that is susceptible to oxidation by a strong chemical oxidant.

q: 225. The activated sludge
explain: Activated sludge is rich in nutrients (N and P), its color/smell indicates aeration levels, and it typically has a very high water content (>95%).

q: 226. Sludge treatment is mainly done in order of
explain: The goals of sludge treatment are to make it non-putrescible (stable), kill germs, and reduce its volume for easier disposal.

q: 227. Of the total content of water on globe the available quantity for use is less than
explain: While much of the globe is water, most is saline or frozen; accessible freshwater for human use is a tiny fraction of the total.

q: 228. Water for domestic consumption should be
explain: The most critical requirement for drinking water is that it be 'potable' or hygienically safe (free from disease-causing pathogens).

q: 229. A pollutant is
options: any foreign element in excess concentration
an element causing change in quality
explain: In environmental engineering, a substance becomes a pollutant when its concentration is high enough to cause undesirable effects.

q: 230. For good taste a desirable temperature of water is
explain: Cooler water (usually < 20°C) is more palatable and generally preferred for domestic consumption.

q: 231. A hot water or waste water sample may have
explain: Increased temperature speeds up metabolic rates and chemical reactions, leading to higher biological activity.

q: 232. True colour of water is due to
explain: True colour is caused by dissolved or colloidal materials (like humic acids); apparent colour is caused by suspended matter.

q: 233. A source of colour in water is due to
explain: Decomposing organic debris (leaves, wood) releases tannins and humic substances that colour the water.

q: 234. Purest water may have
explain: Because water molecules absorb red light more than blue, very pure, deep water often appears to have a faint blue or green tint.

q: 235. Highly coloured waters are
explain: While color might not always mean danger, it is 'unaesthetic'—consumers will likely reject it based on its appearance.

q: 236. An industry that insists on colour free water is
explain: The tanning industry requires high-quality, colour-free water to prevent staining or affecting the quality of the leather.

q: 237. Coloured waters may affect the following water treatment unit
explain: Colouring matter can react with chlorine, exerting a chlorine demand and potentially forming disinfection by-products.

q: 238. Permissible colour for drinking water is not more than
explain: Standard drinking water guidelines typically set the limit for colour at 10 to 15 True Colour Units (TCU).

q: 239. If treated water when reaches the consumer is coloured, it is due to
explain: If the water was clear at the plant but coloured at the tap, it often indicates the pickup of rust (iron) from corroding distribution pipes.

q: 240. An equivalent of mg/l is
explain: In water treatment, 1 mg/L is numerically equivalent to 1 part per million (ppm), as 1 liter of water weighs approximately 1 million milligrams.

q: 241. Turbidity for domestic water is undesirable because it
explain: Turbidity makes water look cloudy or 'muddy,' which makes it visually unappealing (unaesthetic) to consumers.

q: 242. For a river in flash flood, turbidity is mainly due to
explain: Flash floods wash large amounts of clay, silt, and soil (inorganic matter) into the river system.

q: 243. Turbidity depends on the presence of the following in water
options: any material capable of preventing light
explain: Turbidity is an optical property; it refers to anything that scatters or absorbs light as it passes through the water.

q: 244. Turbidity is mainly due to
explain: Suspended solids (silt, clay, etc.) are the primary contributors to measurable turbidity.

q: 245. Turbidity is the ability of water to
explain: Turbidity is fundamentally a measurement of light scattering caused by particles in the water.

q: 246. Turbidity is measured by the
options: concentration of colloidal and suspended solids
difference in suspended solids before and after
explain: Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU) are determined by measuring the intensity of light scattered at 90 degrees.

q: 247. The standard unit of turbidity is produced when
options: 1 mg of silicon dioxide in 1 litre of distilled water
1 mg of platinum in 1 litre of distilled water
1 mg of sodium chloride in 1 litre of distilled water
1 mg of cobalt in 1 litre of distilled water
explain: One unit of turbidity is traditionally defined as the turbidity produced by 1 mg of fine silica ($SiO_2$) in 1 liter of pure water.

q: 248. Units of turbidity are
explain: NTU (Nephelometric Turbidity Units) is the standard modern unit for turbidity measurement.

q: 249. Turbidity is undesirable because it
explain: High turbidity blocks sunlight, which inhibits the growth of aquatic plants and algae by preventing photosynthesis.

q: 250. Turbidity can be removed by
explain: The combination of chemical coagulation (clumping small particles together) and filtration is the standard method for removing turbidity.

q: 251. Due to highly turbid waters efficiency of the following operation gets affected
explain: High turbidity leads to rapid clogging of filter beds (especially rapid sand filters), requiring frequent backwashing and reducing overall efficiency.

q: 252. Tastes along with odours are produced in natural waters due to
explain: Decomposing organic matter, algae, and metabolic by-products of microorganisms are the primary sources of unpleasant tastes and odours in water.

q: 253. If 20 ml of an odours water sample is needed 180 ml of odour free distilled water produce 200 ml of odour free mixture, then the threshold odour number (TON) is
explain: TON is calculated as (Volume of Sample + Volume of Distilled Water) / Volume of Sample. Here, $(20 + 180) / 20 = 10$.

q: 254. Water for domestic use should have
explain: While 'no smell' is ideal, the practical standard for domestic water is that it must be 'inoffensive' to the consumer.

q: 255. Conductivity represents the concentration of the following in the water sample
explain: Electrical conductivity is a direct measure of the ability of water to conduct electricity, which is provided by dissolved inorganic ions (solids).

q: 256. Conductivity directly depends on
explain: Only ions (charged particles) contribute to conductivity; non-ionized dissolved substances like sugar or some organics do not.

q: 257. Conductivity reflect
options: compounds which readily dissociate in solution
explain: Conductivity measures electrolytes—compounds like salts, acids, and bases that dissociate into ions when dissolved in water.

q: 258. Conductivity is standardized at
explain: Because conductivity varies with temperature, measurements are typically reported at a standard reference temperature of 25°C.

q: 259. Suspended solids are less in ground water because
options: they are absorbed by the soil
they are filtered through the soil layers
they are set floating on water
they readily settle to the bottom
explain: As water percolates through the earth to reach the water table, soil layers act as a natural sand filter, removing suspended particles.

q: 260. The usual size of suspended solids is
explain: Suspended solids generally range from 1 μm to 100 μm; particles smaller than 1 μm are typically classified as colloids.

q: 261. Suspended solids are undesirable in domestic waters because they
explain: Suspended solids make water look dirty or muddy, which is primarily an aesthetic concern for the user.

q: 262. Non-filterable residue of a water sample represent
explain: Non-filterable residue is the material captured on a standard filter paper, which by definition constitutes the suspended solids.

q: 263. Volatile solids represent
explain: Volatile solids are those that burn off at high temperatures (550-600°C), representing the organic fraction of the solids.

q: 264. A water sample is termed turbid when it
options: fails to transmit light through it
is rich in both suspended and colloidal solids
explain: Turbidity is an optical property where light is scattered or absorbed rather than transmitted in straight lines.

q: 265. The content of total solids in drinking water shall not be greater than
explain: WHO and various national standards usually set 500 mg/L as the desirable limit for Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) in drinking water.

q: 266. If a sample is heated to 600°C, the fraction getting evaporated represents
explain: Heating to 600°C combusts the organic matter; the weight lost represents the volatile solids.

q: 267. pH of water sample containing 0.0001 (10^-1) g of H ion per litre is
explain: pH is defined as $-log_{10}[H^+]$. If $[H^+] = 10^{-1}$, then $pH = 1$.

q: 268. pH of a water sample is 7 pH of another water sample quantity is 8, then pH of the mixture is
explain: pH is logarithmic; you must average the hydrogen ion concentrations, not the pH numbers. The result is always closer to the lower pH value.

q: 269. Higher pH for water is undesirable because
options: it corrodes zinc, copper and lead pipes
it promotes growth of iron and sulphur bacteria
explain: At high pH (>8.5), the efficiency of chlorine as a disinfectant decreases because the hypochlorous acid (HOCl) dissociates into the less effective hypochlorite ion (OCl-).

q: 270. A desirable pH value for domestic water is
explain: A slightly alkaline range (7 to 8.5) is generally preferred to prevent corrosion while ensuring effective disinfection.

q: 271. Alkalinity in natural waters is due to
options: salts of weak bases strong acids
explain: Algae consume CO2 during photosynthesis, which can shift the chemical equilibrium and increase the pH/alkalinity of the water.

q: 272. The two alkalinities which do not co-exist are
explain: Bicarbonate ($HCO_3^-$) and Hydroxide ($OH^-$) ions react with each other to form carbonate ($CO_3^{2-}$), so they cannot exist together in significant amounts.

q: 273. Caustic alkalinity is because of
explain: Caustic alkalinity refers specifically to the alkalinity contributed by hydroxide ($OH^-$) ions.

q: 274. Phenolphthalein end point represents
explain: Titrating to the phenolphthalein end point (pH 8.3) measures all the hydroxide and exactly half of the carbonate alkalinity.

q: 275. A minimum amount of ............... mg/l of alkalinity is desirable in any water
explain: A minimum alkalinity of 20 mg/L as $CaCO_3$ is often recommended to provide 'buffering capacity' to keep pH stable.

q: 276. Excess alkalinity is undesirable in swimming pools because
options: lacrimal fluid around the eye is altered
explain: High alkalinity can alter the pH of the fluid around the eyes, leading to stinging and irritation for swimmers.

q: 277. Excess alkalinity causes CHLOROSIS in plants because of
options: preparation of iron as iron hydroxide
explain: High alkalinity causes iron to precipitate as insoluble iron hydroxide, making it unavailable to the plant for chlorophyll production.

q: 278. Because of excess alkalinity
explain: Highly alkaline water tends to be scale-forming, leading to the buildup of calcium carbonate deposits (incrustations) inside pipes.

q: 279. Due to the photosynthetic activity of algae pH of pools of water
explain: During the day, algae remove $CO_2$ for photosynthesis, which reduces acidity and causes the pH to rise.

q: 280. pH range of mineral acidity is
explain: Mineral acidity (caused by strong acids like $H_2SO_4$ or $HCl$) is present when the pH is below 4.5.

q: 281. pH range of CO2 acidity is
explain: Acidity due to dissolved carbon dioxide (weak acid) typically occurs in the pH range between 4.5 and 8.3.

q: 282. Excess acidity causes
explain: Acidic water (low pH) is aggressive and corrosive, attacking metal pipes and concrete structures.

q: 283. Chloride that is insoluble in water is
explain: Silver chloride ($AgCl$) is famously insoluble and forms a white precipitate, which is the basis for the Mohr's method of chloride testing.

q: 284. Salty taste is mainly due to
explain: Sodium chloride ($NaCl$) is the primary compound responsible for the 'salty' taste in brackish or contaminated water.

q: 285. Laxative effect is because of
explain: Magnesium sulphate ($MgSO_4$), commonly known as Epsom salt, has a well-known laxative effect on humans.

q: 286. A buffer is that
explain: A buffer solution is a system that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

q: 287. A minimum amount of D.O. desirable in any water body is
explain: While 4 mg/L is a survival limit, 5 mg/L is generally considered the desirable minimum to support a healthy and diverse aquatic ecosystem.

q: 288. In a D.O. test oxygen is replaced by equivalent in
explain: In the Winkler method, dissolved oxygen reacts to eventually release an equivalent amount of iodine, which is then titrated.

q: 289. Sodium azide is added to the D.O. test to neutralize the effect of
explain: Nitrites interfere with the Winkler D.O. test; sodium azide is added (Azide Modification) to eliminate this interference.

q: 290. Greater D.O. is undesirable in
explain: Dissolved oxygen in boiler feed water causes severe 'pitting' corrosion of the metal at high temperatures.

q: 291. Supersaturation of any water with D.O. causes
explain: If water is supersaturated with dissolved gases, bubbles can form in the blood and tissues of fish, similar to 'the bends' in divers.

q: 292. B.O.D. represents
options: pollution strength of an organic fraction
pollution strength of bio-degradable organic fraction
explain: BOD measures the amount of oxygen required by bacteria to stabilize the *biodegradable* organic matter in water.

q: 293. B.O.D. equation is
explain: The standard first-order reaction equation for BOD exerted at time t is $L_t = L(1 - 10^{-kt})$, where L is the ultimate BOD.

q: 294. In the B.O.D. equation K is called
explain: The constant 'k' (or 'K') represents the rate at which the organic matter is being oxidized (deoxygenation rate).

q: 295. For ordinary domestic sewage B.O.D. reaction is expected to get completed in about
explain: At 20°C, it takes approximately 20 days to complete the first stage (carbonaceous) of the BOD reaction.

q: 296. Usual population equivalent of B.O.D. is
explain: Population equivalent is used to compare industrial waste to domestic sewage; 80g of BOD per person per day is a common design value.

q: 297. B.O.D. test is standardized at
explain: The standard lab test for BOD is conducted at 20°C for a duration of 5 days ($BOD_5$).

q: 298. Light is excluded in B.O.D. incubator to
explain: If light enters, algae will grow and produce oxygen via photosynthesis, which would give a false, lower BOD reading.

q: 299. The effluent of a biological treatment unit should have a B.O.D. less than
explain: Standard secondary treatment regulations (like the Royal Commission Standard) often require an effluent BOD of 30 mg/L or less.

q: 300. B.O.D. test is not well suited to industrial wastes because
explain: Many industrial wastes contain toxic substances that kill the bacteria used in the test, making the BOD appear much lower than the actual pollution strength.
